name: Madcow 5x5

lead: Madcow 5x5 is a barbell strength program built around the squat, bench press and barbell row, trained three days a week on a heavy, light, medium pattern. It adapts the 5x5 routines of strength coach Bill Starr and was written by a forum poster known as Madcow roughly two decades ago.

For looks, the payoff is muscle. Heavy compound lifting drives growth in the legs, back, chest and shoulders, which is the frame many people in lifestyle and physique circles are trying to build. Strength sites describe it as aimed at intermediate lifters who have stalled on beginner programs; it is documented in training write-ups rather than clinical trials.

paras: Lifters train Monday, Wednesday and Friday, with a rest day between sessions. Day one is squat, bench and row for five reps, day two is a lighter squat with overhead press and deadlift, and day three is squat, bench and row at three reps with heavier loads. Weights are set from a one-rep max and rise weekly in small percentage steps. Programs usually run for a block of weeks to a few months before the weights become too demanding.

Risks are those of heavy barbell training: technique-related strain or injury and fatigue as loads climb. Write-ups say it is not meant for beginners and that it is not a bodybuilding program, so accessory work for arms and shoulders is added by lifters who want it. Advanced lifters are described as getting limited gains from it.

web.title: Madcow 5x5: Workout Program for Intermediate Lifters - StrengthLog

chain: Heavy compound lifts three days a week
Strength and muscle gain in legs, back and chest
angle.text: The program supplies progressive heavy lifting on the squat, bench and row. Muscle added in those movements broadens the back, chest and thighs, which people use as a foundation for physique goals.

lead: Madcow 5x5 is an intermediate strength training program built on three full-body barbell sessions a week, centred on the squat, bench press and barbell row, with overhead press and deadlift in the lighter session [1]. It is derived from the 5x5 template Bill Starr described in his 1976 book The Strongest Shall Survive, modified by a forum user posting as Madcow [1][2].

People use it to put on muscle and strength in the large muscle groups that shape the torso and legs, which is the basis of a fuller, more muscular physique. It is typically recommended in training write-ups to lifters who can no longer add weight every session on a novice program [1].
No clinical trials have tested Madcow 5x5 by name; the surrounding research is general resistance-training literature.
infobox: Squat, bench press, barbell row, overhead press, deadlift [1]
Weekly increase of about 2.5 percent on a heavy-light-medium wave [1]

paras: According to StrengthLog, the first session consists of squat, bench press and barbell row for five reps, the second of a lighter squat for two sets of five, overhead press and deadlift, and the third of squat, bench and row for three reps at a heavier load [1]. Each exercise has warm-up sets leading to the top set [1]. Training days are usually Monday, Wednesday and Friday, though any schedule with a rest day between sessions is described as acceptable [1].
Training weights are calculated from one-rep maxima and increase by about 2.5 percent a week in a heavy, light, medium wave [1].

The template comes from Bill Starr's 1976 book The Strongest Shall Survive [2]. The adapted version was posted on the EliteFitness forum by a poster using the name Madcow, who made changes to Starr's template [2]. StrengthLog notes the original version included power cleans every workout and no deadlifts, whereas the common version trains rows and deadlifts [1].

StrengthLog describes the program as meant for intermediate lifters and lifters returning from a break, and says it is not meant for beginners [1]. It notes limits: it is not a bodybuilding program, the deadlift is trained once a week, bench volume is lower than in dedicated powerlifting programs, and the weights eventually become too heavy, so it usually runs for several months [1].
Lifters who want more arm, shoulder or upper-chest work add accessory exercises, which the default template leaves optional [1].
No studies found. Research on resistance training in general, including heavier loads and weekly progression, exists separately but has not evaluated this program.

timeline.event: Bill Starr publishes The Strongest Shall Survive, source of the 5x5 template [2].
A forum poster known as Madcow posts the adapted intermediate program [1][2].
